suggestions.rationale: Depression is a recognized psychological comorbidity in psoriatic arthritis. A PsA-specific overview of systematic reviews reported pooled depression prevalence across included reviews of approximately 11.9% to 20% and also identified incident depression data. These population-level findings support condition-specific research of the PsA/depression relationship, but they do not establish that PsA caused or aggravated an individual depressive disorder; chronology, disease burden, treatment, and competing psychiatric or medical contributors remain essential.
evidenceGaps: Qualified diagnosis of a depressive disorder rather than symptom-screening results alone
Chronology comparing depressive-disorder onset or worsening with PsA diagnosis, inflammatory activity, pain, functional limitation, and treatment
Documentation of PsA disease burden, including pain, function, skin disease where relevant, and treatment response
Evaluation of alternative psychiatric, medical, medication-related, psychosocial, substance-use, and sleep-related contributors
Qualified rheumatology or mental-health opinion addressing the individual relationship if causation or aggravation is asserted

sourceReferences.citation: Hernández-Rodríguez et al., Rheumatology International (2024), PMID 38797775
sourceReferences.note: PsA-specific overview of systematic reviews found depression among commonly reported psychological comorbidities, with pooled depression prevalence of approximately 11.9% to 20% across included reviews and an incidence estimate where available. Supports comorbidity/association and screening relevance, not individual causation.
sourceReferences.sourceLocator: PMID 38797775; abstract: overview of systematic reviews; pooled depression prevalence 11.9%-20% and depression incidence 21.3 per 1000 person-years
